title: 56% of Recent Home Sellers Used Recording Devices During Showings
summary: Nearly two-thirds of consumers would be likely to keep recording devices active during showings if they were selling a home.

# 56% of Recent Home Sellers Used Recording Devices During Showings


Written by


[Maggie Gunara](https://www.lendingtree.com/writer/maggie-gunara/)


Edited by


[Dan Shepard](https://www.lendingtree.com/writer/dan-shepard/)


Updated Jul 27, 2026


We are committed to providing accurate content that helps you make informed money decisions. Our partners have not commissioned or endorsed this content. Read oureditorial guidelines here .


Buying a home (especially for the[first time](https://www.lendingtree.com/home/mortgage/first-time-home-buyer-programs/) ) has always felt high-stakes, but a LendingTree survey of 2,000 U.S. consumers suggests buyers may feel additional pressure as home surveillance becomes more common.


A significant 56% of recent home sellers say recording devices were active during their most recent home sale or listing, and buyers are noticing. However, that awareness appears to influence buyer behavior, potentially adding another layer of stress to an already high-pressure process.


Here’s a closer look.


Key findings


- **Recording devices are common during home showings.** Nearly three-quarters of recent buyers (72%) say they’ve seen or suspected cameras, microphones or recording devices during a home tour. Among recent sellers, 56% say recording devices were active during their most recent home sale or listing.
- **Many Americans would use recording devices themselves, but buyers have concerns.** Nearly two-thirds of consumers (62%) say they would be likely to keep recording devices active during showings if they were selling a home. However, 64% of recent buyers say they’re concerned about sellers watching, listening to or recording them during home tours.
- **Concerns about being recorded affect buyer behavior.** More than 1 in 5 recent buyers say they avoided discussing their budget or offer strategy (22%), hid their excitement about a home (22%) or avoided saying what they disliked (21%) because of concerns about being recorded.
- **For some buyers, recording devices affected their willingness to move forward.** Nearly 1 in 5 (19%) say they’ve left a showing because of recording devices, and 18% say they decided not to make an offer. Meanwhile, 34% of Americans say knowing recording equipment was used during a showing would make them less likely to submit an offer.


## Recording devices are common during home showings


Nearly three-quarters (72%) of Americans who’ve bought a home in the past five years say they’ve seen or suspected cameras, microphones or recording devices during a home tour. Among Americans who’ve sold a home in the past five years, 56% say recording devices were active during their most recent home sale or listing.


Many recent buyers have had some advance notice, with 69% saying they were warned that recording devices might be present.


Matt Schulz, LendingTree chief consumer finance analyst and author of “Ask Questions, Save Money, Make More: How to Take Control of Your Financial Life,” says cameras are something buyers should expect.


“Assume you’re on camera the moment you walk through the front door,” he says. “Whether you like it or not, that’s the safest assumption. With that in mind, it makes sense to wait until after you’ve left the property to have any conversations that you wouldn’t want heard by the seller. You don’t want to accidentally weaken your negotiating position. Legally, it gets complicated because recording laws vary by state, especially when audio is involved. Sellers should make sure they’re following state law, and buyers should know they may have fewer privacy expectations in someone else’s home than they might assume.”


## Many would use devices themselves, but buyers have concerns


There’s a notable tension between how buyers feel about being recorded and what they say they’d do if the tables were turned. Nearly two-thirds of Americans (62%) say they’d be likely to keep recording devices active during showings if they were selling a home.


Parents and high earners are especially likely to say so, with 79% of those with children younger than 18 and 72% of six-figure earners saying they’d keep recording devices active as sellers. Younger adults are also more likely to say so, including 70% among Gen Zers ages 18 to 29 and 66% among millennials ages 30 to 45.


Yet 64% of recent buyers say they’re at least somewhat concerned about sellers watching, listening to or recording them during home tours.


Schulz says the contrast isn’t surprising. “It’s all about perspective,” he says. “When you’re the seller, cameras feel like security. When you’re the buyer, they can feel like surveillance. Many sellers are thinking about protecting their home and belongings. Most buyers are wondering, ‘Is every word I say being used against me?’ Those are both understandable reactions.”


## Possible recordings change buyer behavior


Cameras alter what buyers say and do inside homes. More than 1 in 5 recent buyers avoided discussing their budget or offer strategy (22%), hid their excitement about a home (22%) or avoided saying what they disliked (21%) because of concerns about being recorded.


Schulz says buyers are right to be concerned. “That’s because even small amounts of extra information can affect negotiations, and that’s not what any buyer wants,” he says. “The best and simplest solution is to just keep quiet while you’re in the house. During the showing, focus on evaluating the home. After the showing, discuss what it’s worth to you and how you want to[negotiate](https://www.lendingtree.com/home/mortgage/how-to-negotiate-a-home-purchase/) , but do it well away from any recording devices.”


### Cameras may change seller behavior, too


Cameras are often used for security, but buyers may have reason to be cautious because many sellers use the recordings to shape how they sell. Among the 89 recent sellers surveyed who had recording devices active during their most recent home sale or listing, the top reasons for using them were monitoring vacant property (61%), protecting the home or valuables (43%) and knowing who entered the home (42%). They also cited the following reasons:


- To comply with insurance or security requirements (39%)
- To monitor pets, children or deliveries (35%)
- To decide whether to make repairs, changes or staging updates (21%)
- Because the devices are usually on and they didn’t think about turning them off (19%)
- To understand what buyers liked or disliked about the home (19%)
- To learn how interested buyers seemed (18%)
- To gather information that could help during negotiations (18%)
- To hear what their real estate agent said about the home (6%)


Among those 89 sellers, 82% reviewed recordings after showings, and nearly half say what they saw influenced negotiations (45%), repairs or staging (43%) or pricing (35%).


Most sellers also say buyers were made aware of the recording devices. Among those 89 sellers, 85% say buyers were told recording devices might be active, and 82% say the cameras were very or somewhat obvious during showings.


## For some recent buyers, cameras are a deal-breaker


Recording devices have prompted some recent buyers to end the homebuying process. Nearly 1 in 5 (19%) say they’ve left a showing because of recording devices, and 18% say they decided not to make an offer. More broadly, 34% of Americans say knowing recording equipment was used during a showing would make them less likely to submit an offer.


However, in a hypothetical where they found out they’d been secretly recorded during a home showing, 24% of Americans would still consider buying the home with no change — and 17% would still consider it but would trust the seller less.


Schulz believes cameras matter, but they aren’t necessarily a reason to walk away.


“If you’re uncomfortable about them, keep the tour brief and largely quiet and then share your thoughts and strategize elsewhere,” he says. “If the home is otherwise a great fit, I don’t think it makes sense to walk away over something that’s relatively easy to manage. However, if the presence of recording devices genuinely makes you uneasy, it’s OK to move on. Buying a home is a huge financial commitment, and you shouldn’t feel pressured into a situation that makes you uncomfortable.”


## Staying financially focused during the buying process in the age of surveillance


When touring homes, it’s easy to get distracted by unexpected factors like security cameras or smart home devices. While those may make a showing feel uncomfortable, buyers should remember that the ultimate goal is finding a home that fits their budget, lifestyle and long-term financial plans. Consider these tips:


- **Keep your eye on the ball.** “Yes, having cameras present can make things a little awkward or weird,” Schulz says. “However, in most cases, that discomfort probably shouldn’t be the deciding factor in a buying decision. At the end of the day, surveillance is temporary, but the right house could be with you for decades.”
- **Stick to your financial priorities.** Before you start touring homes, establish a clear[budget](https://www.lendingtree.com/home/mortgage/how-much-house-can-i-afford-calculator/) and a list of must-have features. Referring back to those priorities after each showing can help keep emotional reactions from overshadowing the factors that matter most to your long-term finances.
- **Evaluate the home beyond the showing.** Remember that a home tour is only one small part of the buying process. Focus on objective considerations like the property’s condition, location, resale potential and[monthly ownership costs](https://www.lendingtree.com/home/mortgage/national-average-monthly-mortgage-payment-and-loan-affordability-in-each-state-ranked/) , as those are the factors that will have the biggest impact long after the cameras are gone.


## Methodology


LendingTree commissioned QuestionPro to conduct an online survey of 2,000 U.S. consumers ages 18 to 80 from June 2 to 11, 2026. The survey was administered using a nonprobability-based sample, and quotas were used to help ensure the sample reflected the overall population. Researchers reviewed all responses for quality control.


We defined generations as the following ages in 2026:


- Generation Z: 18 to 29
- Millennials: 30 to 45
- Generation X: 46 to 61
- Baby boomers: 62 to 80
